lens: facts and integrity: every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution in the published JSON checked against the claims ledger, the ESV copy (46 Scripture quotations re-paired by hand and re-run strict and loose), the BSB chapter files for the sense of every cited reference, the two confession transcriptions (Creeds.json and TCP 1677, re-run by script), Whiston's Josephus, Niese's Greek of Antiquities 18.30 (fetched in this run), and 7 web searches

findings.where: ## When the Text Confronted Its First Hearers, the paragraph beginning "The hostility was old.", last sentence: "After that, Samaritans were kept out of the temple."
findings.problem: (b)/(c) The ledger verifies this from one source: Whiston's eighteenth-century English translation of Antiquities 18.2.2 (Gutenberg #2848: "on which account the Jews afterward excluded them out of the temple"). The Jewish Encyclopedia line it also cites, as the ledger reports it, mentions only the bones. In this run I read the Greek of Antiquities 18.30 in Niese's critical edition (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit, data/tlg0526/tlg001/tlg0526.tlg001.perseus-grc2.xml, fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com). It reads: "ἄνδρες Σαμαρεῖται κρύφα εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἐλθόντες διάρριψιν ἀνθρωπείων ὀστῶν ἐν ταῖς στοαῖς καὶ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἤρξαντο μὴ πρότερον ἐπὶ τοιούτοις νομίζοντες τά τε ἄλλα διὰ φυλακῆς μείζονος ἦγον τὸ ἱερόν." It says the Samaritans scattered human bones in the colonnades and through the whole temple, and that they then 'kept the temple under greater guard'. The sentence breaks off exactly where it would say who was shut out. The words saying Samaritans were barred are not in the critical text: Whiston's "excluded them" follows an older text or a conjecture, and translations differ on this point. Two web searches found no scholarly treatment that settles it. The essay states as flat fact the one detail the Greek does not carry. Both the Greek and Whiston do support the tighter guarding.
findings.fix: Replace "After that, Samaritans were kept out of the temple." with "After that, the temple was guarded more closely." Nothing else changes. The preceding sentence ("...some Samaritans slipped into the Jerusalem temple at Passover, Josephus reports, and threw human remains about its colonnades.") matches the Greek, and the later line "a people his own people despised and blamed for defiling the temple" still rests on the bones episode. Ledger: amend the Josephus line to say the exclusion clause is Whiston's and is absent from Niese's text at 18.30, and that the essay now gives only the stronger guard.

findings.where: excerpt (JSON "excerpt" and the italic standfirst in docs/work/essays/what-the-original-audience-heard.md): "Every book of the Bible was first heard aloud by particular people in a particular place, and reading it well begins with hearing what they heard."
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line. The body shows public reading for the Law (Nehemiah 8; Acts 15:21), Paul's letters (1 Thessalonians 5:27; Colossians 4:16) and Revelation (1:3). It never claims that every book was first received aloud, and it says only "Every book had a first audience". For collected and edited books (Psalms, Proverbs, Kings, Chronicles), no one can say how they were first received. The standfirst claims more than the essay argues.
findings.fix: Change both places to: "Every book of the Bible was first written to particular people in a particular place, and reading it well begins with hearing what they heard." No ledger change is needed beyond a line noting that the standfirst now restates the body's "Every book had a first audience".

findings.where: ## Who the Bible Was First Written To, second paragraph, first sentence: "The crowd at the Water Gate heard the law read to them, and for most of history that is how God's people met the Bible."
findings.problem: (a) Ledger line 60 covers only the first clause (Nehemiah 8:3). The second clause is a broad historical claim with no ledger line. It is sound in substance: the Harris paragraph that follows, Acts 15:21, 1 Thessalonians 5:27 and Revelation 1:3 support it, and mass private reading is recent. But it is unledgered.
findings.fix: No change to the essay. Add a ledger line: "'for most of history that is how God's people met the Bible.' Interpretation, resting on the literacy estimates (Harris, above) and the public-reading passages (Acts 15:21; 1 Thessalonians 5:27; Colossians 4:16; Revelation 1:3)."

findings.where: ## Verses Taken Out of Their Chapters, the paragraph beginning "I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content," he tells them. (Philippians 4:11)
findings.problem: (b)/(g) Still open in the ledger, which leaves it to James's ESV API check. The only ESV text a run actually saw, the 2011 ESV copy, prints the verse without commas: "for I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content." The ledger records that as the original wording for restoring. In this run, two searches that quoted one form or the other simply echoed the query back, so they show nothing. A third, neutral query ("Not that I am speaking of being in need") returned esv.org's text with the commas and an attached footnote letter: "for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be acontent". That looks like scraped page text, and it fits a newer ESV text edition (the ledger notes a Bible Gateway "2025 ESV Text Edition" label). So the restoration test fails: the source that confirms the comma-less form is an older edition, and the current publisher text appears to carry the commas. Note also that other site pieces quote this verse without commas, so the shelf is inconsistent. That is outside this essay. The same 2011-versus-current gap applies in principle to every quotation: the ESV API recheck in "Left for James" is still the closing step.
findings.fix: No change now. If James's ESV API returns Philippians 4:11 without the two commas, restore exactly: "I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content," he tells them.

findings.where: Opening, second paragraph: "Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites told them, \"This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep,\" and then, \"Go your way. ...\" (Nehemiah 8:9–10)"
findings.problem: (c), minor. Nehemiah 8:10 in the ESV begins "Then he said to them": one unnamed speaker (the BSB reads it as Nehemiah). The essay's "and then" makes the whole group speak the joy-of-the-LORD line. The ledger (line 50) notes this and accepts it as allowed by the passage, so the essay and ledger do not conflict. The wording is just looser than the verse.
findings.fix: Optional: replace ", and then, \"Go your way." with ", and one of them went on, \"Go your way." The quotation itself is unchanged.

clean_checks: All 46 Scripture quotations (Closing Texts included) were hand-paired with their verses in this run and re-run against the ESV copy (esv-mdbible, 2011). 45 match strict (punctuation kept) and all 46 match loose. The one strict difference is the two commas in Philippians 4:11, already open in the ledger (finding 4).

LORD/Lord: LORD in Nehemiah 8:9 and 8:10 and "our Lord" in 8:10 follow the ESV. No quoted portion of Amos 1:3, 2:6, Leviticus 19:34 or Micah 6:8 includes the divine name, so nothing else needs small capitals.

Every Scripture quotation carries a reference in the same sentence or paragraph. The bare "the joy of the LORD" lines are callbacks to Nehemiah 8:10, already cited. Trimmed openings ("And all" in Luke 4:22, "for" in Acts 20:27) and trimmed endings (Amos 2:6 at "sandals", Leviticus 19:34 at "Egypt", Hebrews 1:2 at "Son", Romans 13:1 at "authorities") are standard and match the ledger.

BSB sense check (client/public/bible/ch/): every cited reference says what the essay says it does. Nehemiah 6:15, 7:73, 8:1–12; Acts 15:13, 21; 1 Thessalonians 5:27; Colossians 4:15–16; Revelation 1:3; 1 Corinthians 3:4, 16–17; Luke 4:16–29; 2 Kings 5:1; Luke 9:52–55; Luke 10:25–37; John 4:9, 20; Amos 1:1, 3, 6, 9, 11, 13; 2:1, 4, 6–8; 3:2; 5:24; 6:1, 4; 2 Kings 14:11–16, 23, 25; Philippians 1:7, 13, 20–21; 2:25; 4:11–13, 18; Matthew 7:1, 5, 15–16; Romans 13:1, 8; Leviticus 19:34; Micah 6:8; Acts 20:17, 25, 27, 37–38; Hebrews 1:1–2; 2:1; Romans 16:5; Luke 3:1.

Counts and order: Amos's judgments are eight (Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, Israel), so "The eighth judgment fell on the listeners" is right. Luke 9 is "a chapter earlier" than the lawyer of Luke 10:25. "The first two thirds of Micah 6:8" matches the verse's three clauses.
1 Corinthians 3:16 "every 'you' is plural": confirmed from the tagged Greek in the ledger's STEP-data line (2nd person plural verbs, ὑμῖν).

Confession quotations: re-run in this run by script against the TCP keying of the 1677 printing (A34255) and compared by eye with Creeds.json (1689). "necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation", "that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them.", "All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all" and "ordinary means" are exact substrings, capital S included. The closing period after "unto all" in place of the semicolon is ordinary quotation practice. Westminster 1.7 differs only as the ledger says ("observed, for salvation", "the ordinary means", "attain unto"), so "almost exactly" stands.
1677 and 1689, "with the names of their churches attached": consistent with the ledger's CCEL and Monergism results. The TCP 1677 printing has no subscribers, which fits the anonymous first printing.

John Walton (living): the festschrift title and year were reconfirmed by search in this run (For Us, but Not to Us: Essays on Creation, Covenant, and Context in Honor of John H. Walton, Pickwick Publications, Eugene, 2020; editors Miglio, Reeder, J. T. Walton, Way; Biola digital commons, etsjets.org, Wheaton news Feb 2021). The Biola blog says the phrase is in print by 2008. The essay paraphrases him without quotation marks, which is fair and supported.

William Harris (living): Ancient Literacy, 1989. A search in this run returned the 1990 American Archivist review (at best 10 percent for Greece, "perhaps 15 percent" for the Roman Empire) and the 2015 article calling 10 percent the commonly accepted figure. The ledger's Kolb summary has "little more than 10 %". "Not much more than one in ten" sits within these. "Some scholars think he set it too low" is fair (Wright 2015; the BMCR 2019.04.45 review; Horsfall).

Dates and names: fifth century BC for Nehemiah 8; Stephen Langton, English churchman and later archbishop of Canterbury, chapters in the early thirteenth century; Robert Estienne, French printer, Greek New Testament 1551; Geneva Bible 1560 as the first whole English Bible with verse numbers (the 1557 Geneva New Testament explains the essay's "English Bible"); John Hyrcanus and the Gerizim temple late in the second century BC; Coponius governing Judea (6–9 CE) within Jesus' lifetime; Jeroboam son of Joash in the eighth century BC. All match the ledger's sources, and the essay gives no year beyond what they support.

Josephus, the first half of the sentence: Niese's Greek, read in this run, has Samaritans entering Jerusalem secretly at Passover and scattering human bones (ἀνθρωπείων ὀστῶν) in the colonnades (ταῖς στοαῖς) and through the temple, under Coponius. "Threw human remains about its colonnades" is accurate. Only the exclusion sentence is a problem (finding 1).

"Readers have long noticed" the lawyer avoiding "Samaritan": supported by Adam Clarke's commentary (1810–1826), as the ledger quotes it. The Good Samaritan hospitals and laws in all 50 states are supported by the ledger's second-pass search.

Links: /writing/the-bible-assumes-you-will-be-wrong and /writing/how-the-bible-gets-translated-by are in link-targets.json and live in shelf.json. /writing/why-didnt-the-bible-ban-slavery is in link-targets.json and shelf.json as pending, with its rewrite present in client/public/essays/, so it resolves. /study/bible is allowed by BRIEF.md. That is three essay links, inside the two-to-four limit.

First person and biography: "I've written elsewhere" points to James's own Substack chapter. "I have built one too" stays within NOTES.md (a pastor). No title, years in ministry, book count, invented scene or denominational claim.

Fairness: the conservative and progressive passages are handled with the same instrument (each side's memorized verses set against its skipped ones), and the slavery line refers to dead historical figures. No sentence about a living person is unfair or unsupported.
Mechanics: no em-dashes, no exclamation points, and no forbidden-language words (scanned in this run). The published JSON body is identical to the markdown draft below its title and standfirst.

Restorations (g): the ledger's only "Original wording, for restoring" entry is Philippians 4:11, and it does not qualify (finding 4). The writer's cuts were editorial or unsourced (the "two thousand verses" line), so there is nothing else to restore.
